'''Ruth Fitzmayer Schwarz''' (July 12, 1925{{r|boss}} – August 26, 2004) was an American physicist known for her work on [[semiconductor]]s in the electronics industry.{{r|inquirer-obit}}

==Early life and education==
Schwarz was originally from [[Louisville, Kentucky]], where she went to [[Atherton High School, Louisville]], becoming student body president{{r|inquirer-obit}} and graduating with first honors in 1943.{{r|faze}} She stayed in Louisville for undergraduate study at the [[University of Louisville]]. Initially she majored in [[political science]] but she switched to mathematics and science after becoming inspired by a first-year mathematics course{{r|inquirer-obit|faze}} taught there by Walter Lee Moore, the namesake of the university's [[Moore Observatory]].{{r|mixes}}

She went on to [[Harvard University]] for graduate study in physics, working there on the [[magnet]]ic behavior of [[molecule]]s with [[John Hasbrouck Van Vleck]], who later won the Nobel Prize for his work on magnetism.{{r|inquirer-obit}} She earned a master's degree there, through [[Radcliffe College]], in 1949, and completed her Ph.D. in 1953. Her dissertation was ''Rotational magnetic moments in polyatomic molecules''.{{r|faze}}

==Career and later life==
Schwarz became a scientist for transistor manufacturer [[Philco]] in 1952,{{r|inquirer-obit|mixes}} initially modeling the [[Heat transfer|flow of heat]] in their manufacturing processes.{{r|inquirer-obit}} She worked for them in their scientific laboratory in [[Blue Bell, Pennsylvania]],{{r|mixes}} and shifted to part-time work after the birth of her children.{{r|faze|mixes}} In the 1970s she worked in the Space Division of [[General Electric]].{{r|inquirer-obit}}

==Personal life==
Schwarz was the daughter of Lawrence J. Fitzmayer,{{r|mixes}} who taught music at public schools in Louisville{{r|forest-leaves}} and played violin for the [[Louisville Orchestra|Louisville Philharmonic Orchestra]].{{r|faze}} She maintained a lifelong interest in music, playing violin herself in her high school orchestra,{{r|inquirer-obit}} and for nearly three decades with the [[Old York Road Symphony]] beginning circa 1967.{{r|inquirer-obit|blend}}

She met her husband, physicist John Schwarz, at the University of Louisville; they both studied at Harvard, worked at Philco and married in 1950. They had two sons and a daughter.{{r|inquirer-obit|john-obit}}
 
==Recognition==
Philco gave Schwarz their Presidential Special Award.{{r|inquirer-obit}} Schwarz was named a [[Fellow of the American Physical Society]] in 1963.{{r|aps-fellow}}
